column3: A pattern is copied from another project without fitting this one.
column4: Compare the proposal with the existing architecture and conventions.

column3: Excessive abstractions and configuration.
column4: Compare the number of new layers and options with what the requirements need.

column3: A public interface exposes unnecessary implementation details.
column4: Compare what is exported with what its consumers actually use.

column3: Hidden shared state complicates reasoning and tests.
column4: Look for mutable globals, singletons, and implicit dependencies the design introduces or relies on.

column3: An intermediate layer adds no contract or value.
column4: Look for layers that only forward calls without a contract of their own.

column3: A class, module, or equivalent unit combines independent responsibilities or reasons to change.
column4: Compare the responsibility groups of the units the design touches and look for unrelated changes that would repeatedly hit the same unit.

column3: A dependency cycle prevents independent module changes.
column4: Look for import or call cycles between the modules the design touches.

column3: Domain logic leaks into UI, transport, or persistence.
column4: Trace where the design places each rule.

column3: A missing shared mechanism leaves the same mechanics duplicated and unreliable.
column4: Look for the same mechanism implemented in several places where one shared mechanism fits.

column3: A pattern is applied dogmatically without a need.
column4: Compare it with a simpler option and its structural cost.

column3: A public API embeds external provider details.
column4: Trace types and errors that cross the boundary to the provider.

column3: Duplicated state has no consistency rule.
column4: Compare the sources of truth and the points where each copy is updated.

column3: Apparent modularity hides temporal coupling.
column4: Look for components that work only when initialized or called in an order nothing enforces.

column3: The design does not say what its failures do to data and consumers.
column4: Trace what a failure of each new or changed component does to the data and to the components that depend on it.

column3: Migration or future maintenance is ignored.
column4: Where the design changes stored data or public contracts, look for how existing data and consumers are migrated.

column3: A rule or invariant has no unambiguous owning component.
column4: Check that each rule has one component that enforces it, and look for paths that change its state elsewhere.

column3: A component's public interface lets callers bypass its invariants.
column4: Look for public operations through which a caller can break an invariant.

column3: Stable domain rules depend on volatile implementation details.
column4: Check that dependencies point from providers, transport, and storage towards domain rules, not the reverse.

column3: Module boundaries split a cohesive responsibility across components.
column4: Take a representative rule change and count the modules that must change together.

column3: A failure in one component disables unrelated capabilities.
column4: Trace what becomes unavailable when each component fails and compare it with what must keep working.

column3: Domain rules cannot be verified without the full runtime or live external services.
column4: Check that component contracts can be verified with controlled dependencies, and that any required live integration is justified.
